name: CACHE Challenge #3
description: Blinded prospective community challenge in which computational teams select commercially available compounds for a named target, the organisers synthesise and assay them, and confirmed hits are scored by an independent Hit Evaluation Committee.

attributes.task: Prospective hit identification for the SARS-CoV-2 Nsp3 macrodomain (Mac1)
attributes.scope_note: Round 1 (hit identification): each of 23 workflows selected up to 100 commercially available compounds; 1739 were synthesised by Enamine and tested. All 1739 were screened at 100 uM by homogeneous time-resolved fluorescence (HTRF); 302 reduced the binding signal by 30% or more in at least one of two duplicates or gave ambiguous data and went to a limited three-point dose response, then to surface plasmon resonance; 28 advanced to Round 2. In parallel all 1739 were soaked with crystallised Nsp3-Mac1, giving complex structures for 44. Round 2 (hit expansion): up to 50 close analogues per team, 296 compounds tested, 84 confirmed. Teams were also asked to predict actives from the merged library of all 1739 Round 1 compounds, so that every workflow ran on the same library; confirmed hits with a score above 15 were clustered into four chemically novel Tier 1 compounds and 25 Tier 2 compounds.
attributes.source_locator: Results 'Compounds Were Drug-like and Chemically Diverse', 'Discovering Chemically Novel Ligands Was Challenging', 'Selection and Experimental Testing of Round 2 Compounds'; Figure 6 caption
limitations: The challenge scores confirmed hits with an activity score set by a Hit Evaluation Committee and a novelty score voted by three chemists. It does not publish a per-workflow hit rate.

Targets and libraries were chosen by the organisers and predictions were submitted before testing, so there is no training-overlap control in the usual sense; the Nsp3-Mac1 binding features were already well documented, and 61 Mac1 ligands had been published.
Only the published CACHE #3 round is extracted here. The CACHE #1 and #2 results papers (doi 10.1021/acs.jcim.4c01267 and 10.1021/acs.jcim.5c00535) are not open access and were not retrieved.

name: DEKOIS 2.0
description: Virtual-screening benchmark that scores a method on how well it ranks experimentally validated actives above property-matched decoys for each of its targets.

attributes.scope_note: As described by Shen et al. 2025: 81 structurally diverse targets, each with 40 experimentally validated actives from BindingDB and 1200 property-matched decoys selected from ZINC, an actives-to-decoys ratio of 1:30. Data at http://www.dekois.com.
limitations: The decoys are synthetic property-matched molecules, not measured inactives, so enrichment factors on this benchmark are not comparable with benchmarks whose negatives were assayed.

The set was released over ten years before Shen et al. 2025 and its template protein structures may overlap substantially with the training data of the co-folding models scored on it (Results 'Performance on GPCRrecent dataset').

version.note: The DEKOIS 2.0 primary paper (doi 10.1021/ci400115b) is closed access and was not retrieved; the composition recorded here is as Shen et al. 2025 describe it

name: DUD-E (Directory of Useful Decoys, Enhanced)
description: Virtual-screening benchmark that scores ligand enrichment against property-matched decoys for each target.

attributes.version: DUD-E as published in 2012; no release identifier is printed in the abstract

limitations: Chen et al. 2019 report that convolutional neural network models trained on DUD-E can distinguish actives from decoys using artefacts of how the decoys were constructed rather than protein-ligand binding, so DUD-E performance of such models is misleading.

name: GPCRrecent
description: Virtual-screening benchmark of G protein-coupled receptor targets whose first crystal structures were determined after 2022, scoring how well a method ranks BindingDB actives above generated property-matched decoys.

attributes.version: Curated by Shen et al. 2025; data at https://zenodo.org/records/16826965
attributes.scope_note: Built so that the targets are temporally separated from AlphaFold3's training data: targets whose first crystal structure was released after 2022, with BindingDB actives below 10 uM activity, peptide-like inhibitors and natural products above 600 Da excluded, actives clustered on Murcko scaffolds with the most potent representative per cluster kept, at most 300 diverse scaffolds per target and targets with fewer than 200 actives removed; 16 GPCRs result. Decoys are generated by a streamlined TocoDecoy implementation at a 1:50 actives-to-decoys ratio.
attributes.source_locator: Methods 'Datasets'; Results 'Performance on GPCRrecent dataset'; Data availability
limitations: The decoys are generated by a conditional recurrent neural network, not assayed inactives, so enrichment factors are not comparable with benchmarks whose negatives were measured.

Temporal separation holds for crystal structures, not for binding data: the authors exclude the Boltz-2 affinity module from this analysis because its training sources (for example BindingDB) overlap the benchmark's composition.
The per-target composition is in Table S1, which was not retrieved.

name: LIT-PCBA
description: Virtual-screening benchmark whose actives and inactives are both experimentally measured, taken from high-confidence PubChem BioAssay dose-response data.

attributes.version: Full data and AVE-unbiased data as published on the official page; no version string is printed
attributes.scope_note: 15 target sets. The official page states 7761 actives and 382674 unique inactives from high-confidence PubChem BioAssay data, with per-target counts and an AVE-unbiased split published alongside the full data; Shen et al. 2025 state 10030 confirmed actives and 2798737 confirmed inactives for the full set. Because the inactives are measured rather than synthetic, and because the actives-to-inactives ratio reaches about 1:18000 for ADRB2, enrichment factors on LIT-PCBA sit far below those on property-matched decoy benchmarks.
attributes.source_locator: Official page data content table; Shen et al. 2025 Methods 'Datasets'
limitations: Huang, Knight and Naprienko 2025 audit the benchmark and report extensive leakage between its splits: 323 active training-validation analogue pairs at ECFP4 Tanimoto at or above 0.6 in ALDH1 alone, and 2491 2D-identical inactives shared between training and validation across targets. They conclude that a parameter-free memorisation baseline matches or exceeds published deep-learning and 3D-similarity results, that nearly all published LIT-PCBA results are undermined, that zero-shot evaluations are also affected by analogue leakage into the query set, and that the benchmark in its current form does not measure recovery of novel chemotypes.
The official page and Shen et al. 2025 give different active and inactive totals and neither reconciles them.
The LIT-PCBA primary paper (doi 10.1021/acs.jcim.0c00155) is closed access and was not retrieved.

name: LIT-PCBA leakage audit: a parameter-free memorisation baseline matches the state of the art
description: The headline finding of the LIT-PCBA data-leakage audit, which bears on every LIT-PCBA result.

attributes.value: Huang, Knight and Naprienko report extensive data leakage and molecular redundancy across the LIT-PCBA splits: 2D-identical ligands within and across partitions, pervasive analogue overlap and low-diversity query sets. In ALDH1 alone 323 active training-validation analogue pairs occur at ECFP4 Tanimoto at or above 0.6; across all targets 2,491 2D-identical inactives appear in both training and validation, with very few corresponding actives. They state that these overlaps let models succeed through scaffold memorisation rather than generalisation, inflating enrichment factors and AUROC scores, and that the flaws are severe enough that a trivial memorisation-based baseline with no learnable parameters can match or exceed the reported performance of state-of-the-art deep-learning and 3D-similarity models. They conclude that nearly all published results on LIT-PCBA are undermined, that even models evaluated in zero-shot mode are affected by analogue leakage into the query set, and that the benchmark in its current form does not measure a model's ability to recover novel chemotypes.

name: Actives-to-decoys ratio and decoy construction differ by orders of magnitude between the screening benchmarks
description: The composition facts that make raw enrichment factors incomparable between these benchmarks.

attributes.value: DEKOIS 2.0 holds 40 experimentally validated actives and 1200 property-matched decoys selected from ZINC per target, a ratio of 1:30. GPCRrecent holds BindingDB actives with decoys generated by a conditional recurrent neural network (TocoDecoy) at 1:50. LIT-PCBA's negatives are experimentally measured inactives, and its official per-target counts give ratios from 13 actives to 4,378 inactives (ESR_ago, about 1:337) and 88 to 3,820 (ESR_antago, about 1:43) up to 17 to 311,748 (ADRB2, about 1:18,000). DUD-E pairs each of 22,886 clustered ligands with 50 property-matched decoys. An enrichment factor is a ratio against random selection at a fixed fraction of the list, so it moves with both the ratio and the realism of the negatives; values from these benchmarks are not comparable with one another.
attributes.source_locator: Shen et al. 2025 Methods 'Datasets' and 'Evaluation metrics'; LIT-PCBA official page data content table

description: Have every CACHE #3 workflow predict which of the same 1739 Round 1 compounds are active, and count the confirmed Tier 1 and Tier 2 hits among each workflow's predicted actives.

review.reviewer_note: Claude review agent, independent of the extraction agent; no human review claimed

review.note: Record checked against the pinned source and the record contract. Transcription checked; not reproduced and not reviewed by a human scientist.

attributes.metric_qualifier: confirmed hits among one workflow's predicted actives on the merged 1739-compound library
attributes.metric_definition: Every workflow was applied to the merged library of all 1739 Round 1 compounds. Confirmed hits with a score above 15 were clustered into four chemically novel Tier 1 compounds and 25 Tier 2 compounds. Columns L to Q are counts. Columns R, S and T are stored as the formulas 1000*N/L, 1000*O/L and R+S, so they are confirmed Tier 1 or Tier 2 hits per 1000 compounds predicted active; the Figure 6c caption's wording, 'the aggregated score of all compounds predicted active divided by the number of compounds predicted to be actives', does not describe that formula.
attributes.protocol: Complementary evaluation scheme in which all computational workflows are applied to the same chemical library, so that selection of the library does not differ between them.
attributes.version: Herasymenko et al. 2026, Supporting Information table S8
attributes.source_locator: Sheet 'S8' of ci5c02441_si_002.xlsx, merged-library columns; Figure 6 caption
limitations: The library is the union of what the 23 workflows themselves selected, so it is not an independent library and each workflow's own picks are in it.
Four of the 23 workflows (1694, 1695, 1716, 1717) have no values printed in these columns; they are recorded as absent, not as zero.
Only 29 confirmed hits scored above 15, four of them chemically novel, so the Tier 1 counts rest on four compounds in total.

The two normalised columns are labelled as counts of hits while the Figure 6c caption defines the normalised quantity as an aggregated score divided by the number of compounds predicted active. The stored cell formulas (1000*N/L and 1000*O/L) agree with the column labels and not with the caption. The sheet's final column has no printed header at all; its formula is R+S.

Columns L to Q are counts of compounds, not rates. Columns R, S and T are rates: the workbook stores them as 1000*N/L, 1000*O/L and R+S, so each is confirmed Tier 1 or Tier 2 hits per 1000 compounds predicted active. Predicting the merged library is also not the same task as selecting compounds to synthesise.

The article is internally inconsistent about Figure 6. The Results section 'Trends and Strategies from the Best Performing Computational Workflows' calls panels a, b and c 'top scoring compounds, top hit rates, and top selections from the merged Round 1 library', while the Figure 6 caption calls panel b 'the aggregated score of all Round 1 hits' and panel c the normalised Tier 1 and Tier 2 counts. The body text therefore calls an aggregated score a hit rate. No value in this batch is taken from Figure 6; every value is from sheet S8.
attributes.scope_note: Prospective: predictions were submitted before any compound was synthesised or assayed.

attributes.metric_qualifier: compounds selected by one workflow and the confirmed hits among them
attributes.metric_definition: Compounds tested is the number a workflow selected that Enamine synthesised and the organisers assayed. Hits are the experimentally confirmed actives among them. Chemically Novel Hits are those the Hit Evaluation Committee judged novel. The activity score reflects the quality and consistency of the binding signals and the chemical soundness of the molecule, including absence of undesirable groups; the novelty score runs from 0 (not novel) to 3 (unanimously voted as novel) across three independent chemists.
attributes.protocol: Blinded and prospective: each team selected up to 100 commercially available compounds before any testing. All 1739 selected compounds were screened by HTRF at 100 uM, then by a three-point dose response, then by surface plasmon resonance, and in parallel by crystal soaking.
attributes.version: Herasymenko et al. 2026, Supporting Information table S8
attributes.source_locator: Sheet 'S8' of ci5c02441_si_002.xlsx; scoring described in the article's Results and Figure 6 caption
limitations: Each workflow selected its own compounds, so the workflows are not compared on a common library in this arm. The merged-library arm is the comparison on one library.

No hit rate is printed for this arm. Compounds tested (column D) and Hits (column E) are printed as separate counts and this batch records both without dividing them, because a derived rate would be a computation rather than a printed value. The article does publish a per-workflow rate, but for the merged-library arm: columns R, S and T of sheet S8 are stored as the formulas 1000*N/L, 1000*O/L and R+S, that is confirmed Tier 1 or Tier 2 hits per 1000 compounds predicted active.
Workflow numbers of compounds tested range from 41 to 99, so the counts rest on small and unequal denominators.
The activity and novelty scores are committee judgements, not measurements, and the per-compound scoring matrix (sheet S7) was not extracted.
Participants are named for only 10 of the 23 workflows in this sheet; the rest are anonymous.

Twelve of the 23 workflows returned no confirmed hit, and the workbook stores 0 for their score of best hit, aggregated score, top novelty score and top score of novel hits. A 0 in those columns means there was no hit to score, not a hit scored at zero; each affected result carries that warning.

description: Rank the compounds of a tested ultra-large docking hit list by DOCK3.7 energy, AlphaFold3 L-pLDDT or Boltz-2 pIC50, and report the area under the ROC curve for separating measured binders from high-ranking docking false positives.

review.reviewer_note: Claude review agent, independent of the extraction agent; no human review claimed
review.method_note: Read the record against the pinned sources and against docs/use-cases.md and docs/record-contract.md.
review.note: Record checked against the pinned source and the record contract. Transcription checked; not reproduced and not reviewed by a human scientist.

attributes.unit_detail: printed as a percentage on a 0-100 scale
attributes.metric_qualifier: discrimination of measured binders from high-ranking docking false positives in a tested hit list
attributes.metric_definition: Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve for separating true hits from non-binders, printed in the body text as a percentage.
attributes.protocol: Every compound in the list was synthesised and assayed in the original screening campaign. The three scores are then computed for those same compounds and their ranking compared; the comparison itself is a retrospective re-ranking of a prospectively tested set.
attributes.version: Kim, Correy, Hall et al. 2026, Results 'Co-folding struggles to reliably re-rank docking hit lists'
attributes.source_locator: Results 'Co-folding struggles to reliably re-rank docking hit lists'; Methods 'Benchmarking co-folding on experimentally validated compounds'
attributes.control: DOCK3.7, the engine that produced the hit list, is scored on the same compounds.
limitations: The negatives are compounds a docking screen already ranked highly, which is a far harder and more realistic negative set than property-matched decoys; these AUC values are not comparable with enrichment on decoy benchmarks.
The list is a biased sample of the library: only high-ranking docked molecules were synthesised, so neither the AUC nor any hit rate derived from it estimates performance over a whole library.

No training-overlap control is stated for this arm. Training cutoffs are given for the separate Mac1 pose benchmark, and Supplementary file 2 reports pairwise similarity between the datasets, but neither was extracted here.
The hit-rate curves, the semi-logarithmic ROC curves and the early-enrichment values for these sets are published only as figures (Figure 5 and its supplements 3 and 4) and were not read.

attributes.metric_qualifier: mean and median over the DEKOIS 2.0 targets
attributes.metric_definition: AUROC, BEDROC with alpha = 80.5 (the top 2% of the ranked list contributes 80% of the score), and enrichment factors at 0.5%, 1% and 5%, each reported as the mean and the median over targets. EFx% is the ratio of true positives found in the top x% of the ranked compounds relative to random selection.
attributes.protocol: Co-folding from protein sequence and ligand SMILES with pre-computed MSAs, then ranking by the model's own confidence score; docking tools rank the same compounds for the same targets.
attributes.version: Shen et al. 2025, Table 1

limitations: Enrichment factors depend on the actives-to-inactives ratio and on how the negatives were built, which differ by more than an order of magnitude between the benchmarks in this store (1:30 for DEKOIS 2.0, 1:50 for GPCRrecent, and from about 1:43 to about 1:200 across the five LIT-PCBA targets scored here, reaching about 1:18000 for LIT-PCBA ADRB2). Values from different protocols are not comparable.
The decoys are property-matched synthetic molecules, not assayed inactives.
Eight of the 24 rows are quoted from other papers (footnotes b to f: refs 34, 35, 36, 38 and 39), so they were not run under one common pipeline; none of those references was retrieved in this pass.
The SurfDock row's indicators were calculated on all 81 targets rather than the 79 used elsewhere in the table, because the per-target labels were unavailable (footnote f).

The authors warn that the Boltz-2 Affinity and Probability rows are likely to be significantly over-estimated because Boltz-2 fetched affinity data from the public databases that also source DEKOIS 2.0, and they exclude those two rows from their own primary comparison (footnote a and Methods 'Affinity score and probability').

Values from different protocols are not comparable.

Huang, Knight and Naprienko 2025 audit LIT-PCBA and conclude that analogue and 2D-identical-compound leakage between its splits lets a parameter-free memorisation baseline match or exceed published results, that nearly all published LIT-PCBA results are undermined, and that the benchmark does not measure recovery of novel chemotypes. That bears on every value from this protocol.

Five of the 15 LIT-PCBA targets were screened, chosen for size; MTORC1 meets the size criterion but was excluded for ambiguous binding sites, which is a selection the authors made rather than a property of the benchmark.

name: Summary of the evidence for use-case-hit-discovery-virtual-screening
description: Draft summary of what the extracted evidence shows. Descriptive only, not reviewed.

attributes.value:
Three sources in this store score machine-learning and co-folding methods against docking on the same screening data, and what the numbers say depends on how the negatives were built.

On DEKOIS 2.0, whose 79 targets each pair 40 validated actives with 1,200 property-matched decoys selected from ZINC (1:30), the co-folding confidence scores enrich strongly and beat the docking arms. AF3 min-iPAE gives a mean EF1% of 23.15 and Boltz-2 min-iPAE 22.73, against 12.01 for the Glide SP row quoted from another paper, 5.16 for Gnina Vina and 2.94 for TankBind; the best rescoring of a co-folded pose, RTMScore on AF3 poses, reaches 21.34. The authors flag their own Boltz-2 affinity arms (mean EF1% 23.54 and 25.84) as likely over-estimates because Boltz-2 drew affinity data from the same public databases that source DEKOIS 2.0.

On GPCRrecent, 16 targets whose first crystal structures were released after 2022 with decoys generated by a conditional recurrent neural network at 1:50, every value falls and the margin narrows: Boltz-2 min-iPAE gives a mean EF1% of 13.96 against 5.02 for Glide SP and 3.65 for Gnina Vina. On the five LIT-PCBA targets where the inactives were experimentally measured, the margin largely disappears: averaged over the five targets Boltz-2 min-iPAE gives EF1% 9.30 and NEF1% 0.100 against Glide SP's 6.79 and 0.079, and on TP53 both Boltz-2 scores give EF1% 0.00 while Protenix ipTM gives 5.00 and Glide SP 3.75. A separate audit of LIT-PCBA reports 323 active training-validation analogue pairs at ECFP4 Tanimoto at or above 0.6 in ALDH1 alone and 2,491 2D-identical inactives shared between training and validation across targets, and concludes that a parameter-free memorisation baseline matches or exceeds published deep-learning results there, so every LIT-PCBA value above carries that limit.

Where the negatives are compounds a docking screen already ranked highly and every compound was synthesised and assayed, the ordering changes. On the AmpC list (247 inhibitors among 1,293 tested compounds from a 1.7-billion molecule screen) DOCK3.7 separates binders best, AUC 76.5, against 68.1 for Boltz-2 pIC50 and 60.5 for AF3 L-pLDDT. On the dopamine D4 list (205 binders among 541) docking and Boltz-2 are indistinguishable at the precision printed (both about 71) and AF3 L-pLDDT is worse than random at 46.4. Only on the sigma-2 list (201 binders among 506) does a co-folding score lead, Boltz-2 pIC50 at 83.8 against DOCK3.7's 78.8, with AF3 L-pLDDT at 56.1.

In the one blinded prospective challenge, CACHE #3 on the SARS-CoV-2 Nsp3 macrodomain, 23 workflows selected 1,739 compounds that were synthesised and assayed; 28 advanced to hit expansion and 29 confirmed hits scored above 15, four of them judged chemically novel. Twelve of the 23 workflows returned no confirmed hit from their own selection of 41 to 99 compounds. When every workflow was applied to the same merged 1,739-compound library, WF1696, which the article describes as a purely physics-based method, captured 2 of the 4 Tier 1 and 9 of the 25 Tier 2 confirmed hits from 99 predicted actives, which the authors report as did better than any other method in retrieving hits from the collection of all molecules selected in Round 1.

Cost bounds all of this: co-folding one protein-ligand pair takes 7.79 to 34.58 seconds per compound on one NVIDIA H100 with pre-computed MSAs, which is why the LIT-PCBA arm covers five targets rather than fifteen. No docking tool was timed on the same hardware, no ligand-similarity or pharmacophore baseline is scored anywhere in this batch, and no result here estimates the hit rate of an untested library.

name: Find hits for a target by virtual screening
description: Which computational screening workflow puts real binders at the top of a large compound library, and how many compounds must be tested to find one?

attributes.question: Which computational screening workflow puts real binders at the top of a large compound library, and how many compounds must be tested to find one?
intended_users: Computational chemists choosing a scoring method before committing a library screen to synthesis and assay
Project teams deciding how many top-ranked compounds to buy or make, and what hit rate to expect
Method developers who need to know which screening benchmarks can still distinguish methods
attributes.decision: Choose the method that will rank a compound library for one protein target, and decide how many top-ranked compounds to synthesise and test.
inputs: One protein target, with a sequence and, for docking and rescoring methods, a prepared receptor structure
A compound library to rank, with the actives-to-inactives ratio and how any negatives were constructed
A compute budget, since cost per compound decides whether a method can run on the library at all
A synthesis and assay budget, which sets how many top-ranked compounds can be tested
attributes.output: Enrichment of true actives at a stated fraction of the library for each method on each protocol, with the decoy construction and actives-to-inactives ratio of that protocol; measured counts of confirmed hits and compounds tested where a paper synthesised and assayed compounds; and compute per compound. No recommendation of a method and no prediction of a hit rate for an untested library.
attributes.setting: Early hit discovery for a single protein target with a known or predictable structure. The endpoint is the ranking of a library, not the accuracy of one complex: an enrichment factor at a stated fraction of the list, or a measured count of confirmed hits with its denominator. Retrospective benchmarks score a method against a curated set of actives and negatives; prospective campaigns measure what was found when compounds were actually synthesised and assayed. The two answer different questions and are kept apart.
exclusions: Pose accuracy and binding-mode reproduction, including the Mac1 co-folding pose benchmark and the CASF-2016 docking power protocols already in this store
Affinity prediction and scoring-power correlation, including CASF-2016 scoring and ranking power
Lead optimisation and hit-to-lead potency improvement, which is a separate use case
De novo molecule generation and library design
Any recommendation for clinical or therapeutic use
attributes.clinical_scope: Research use only. Nothing here supports a clinical decision, and no compound named in the cited sources is a medicine.
evidence_gaps: No protocol in this store scores a ligand-similarity or pharmacophore search as a pre-machine-learning baseline, although issue #177 asks for one alongside docking. Lam et al. 2024 print IFP and GRIM rows on LIT-PCBA but quote them from third parties.
No DUD-E evaluation is extracted. DUD-E is registered with its composition and the Chen et al. 2019 bias finding, but no result on it is recorded.

No MF-PCBA evaluation is extracted, so the Boltzina and Boltz-2 affinity-head fine-tuning results on measured PubChem dose-response data (arXiv:2508.17555 and arXiv:2609.24302) remain outside the store; only their abstracts were seen in the search pass.
The hit-rate curves, semi-logarithmic ROC curves and early-enrichment values for the three Kim et al. docking hit lists are published only as figures and were not read.

Kawano et al. 2026 report a measured 70% hit rate (28 of 40) at 10 uM for Boltz-2 on an Enamine diversity set, with no docking arm and after score and diversity filtering from a pre-curated library; the authors state it is not an unbiased estimate. It was not extracted in this pass.

DockM8 (Hamza et al. 2026) reports median relative enrichment across DEKOIS 2.0, DUD-E and LIT-PCBA with an AVE-split generalisation check, and Lam et al. 2024 report a sequence-only screening model with a homology-removed zero-shot arm. Neither was extracted; both carry docking baselines on the same data.

CACHE #1 and #2 are not open access and were not retrieved, so two of the three rounds of the best prospective benchmark are missing and nothing here shows whether the CACHE #3 ordering holds across targets.

The paper relating library size and number tested to hit rate (doi 10.1038/s41589-024-01797-w) is not open access and was not retrieved, so the second half of the question, how many compounds must be tested, rests only on the tested denominators recorded here.
No compute-per-compound figure is recorded for any docking tool, so the cost comparison between co-folding and docking is one-sided.
The DEKOIS 2.0, LIT-PCBA and TocoDecoy primary papers are closed access and were not retrieved; their composition is recorded as Shen et al. 2025 and the official LIT-PCBA page describe it.
Qualified human scientific review is outstanding; automated transcription does not establish replication.

On GPCRrecent, 16 targets whose first crystal structures were released after 2022 with decoys generated by a conditional recurrent neural network at 1:50, every value falls and the margin narrows: Boltz-2 min-iPAE gives a mean EF1% of 13.96 against 5.02 for Glide SP and 3.65 for Gnina Vina. Where the negatives are compounds a docking screen already ranked highly and every compound was synthesised and assayed, the ordering changes. On the AmpC list (247 inhibitors among 1,293 tested compounds from a 1.7-billion molecule screen) DOCK3.7 separates binders best, AUC 76.5, against 68.1 for Boltz-2 pIC50 and 60.5 for AF3 L-pLDDT. On the dopamine D4 list (205 binders among 541) docking and Boltz-2 are indistinguishable at the precision printed (both about 71) and AF3 L-pLDDT is worse than random at 46.4. Only on the sigma-2 list (201 binders among 506) does a co-folding score lead, Boltz-2 pIC50 at 83.8 against DOCK3.7's 78.8, with AF3 L-pLDDT at 56.1.

In the one blinded prospective challenge, CACHE #3 on the SARS-CoV-2 Nsp3 macrodomain, 23 workflows selected 1,739 compounds that were synthesised and assayed; 28 advanced to hit expansion and 29 confirmed hits scored above 15, four of them judged chemically novel. Twelve of the 23 workflows returned no confirmed hit from their own selection of 41 to 99 compounds. When every workflow was applied to the same merged 1,739-compound library, WF1696, which the article describes as a purely physics-based method, captured 2 of the 4 Tier 1 and 9 of the 25 Tier 2 confirmed hits from 99 predicted actives, which the authors report as significantly more hits than any other workflow.

Cost bounds all of this: co-folding one protein-ligand pair takes 7.79 to 34.58 seconds per compound on one NVIDIA H100 with pre-computed MSAs, which is why the LIT-PCBA arm covers five targets rather than fifteen. No docking tool was timed on the same hardware, no ligand-similarity or pharmacophore baseline is scored anywhere in this batch, and no result here estimates the hit rate of an untested library.
